CH1 · UNIT 02 · MODULE 2.5

Mutation & DNA Repair

What happens when DNA goes wrong. Part 1: how replication errors and damage from UV, X-rays and chemicals arise, and the repair crews that fix them (proofreading, mismatch repair, base excision, nucleotide excision). Part 2: what a mutation that slips through does to a gene, its mRNA and its protein, from silent to frameshift, with sickle cell and cystic fibrosis. Module 2.4's gene is the one that gets mutated.

MODULE 2.5 · PART 1

Mistakes, and how they get fixed

THE QUESTIONDNA gets copied billions of letters at a time, and battered by UV light, X-rays and chemicals. How does it stay correct?

Seven steps: the life of a mistake, how an error becomes a mutation, proofreading and mismatch repair, kinds of DNA damage, base excision repair, UV and nucleotide excision repair, and the four repair systems side by side.

STEP 1 · THE BIG PICTURE

The life of a mistake

Module 2.4's gene, Met–Glu–Arg–Leu, is about to meet some trouble. Here's every way the story can go.

Tap the buttons, or Next step, to click through all 6
THE LIFE OF A MISTAKEFrom a mistake to a mutationDNA gets damaged, and DNA polymerase sometimes makes errors. Most are fixed. The ones that slip through, and get copied, are mutations. What a mutation does depends on where it is. Tap through.
DAMAGE OR ERRORTwo causesErrors in cellular processes like DNA replication (spontaneous, the most common), or environmental factors (mutagens) like X-rays, UV light and chemicals that damage DNA.Go to this step →
REPAIRCells have lots of repair systemsDNA polymerase proofreads as it goes; mismatch repair catches what it misses; base excision and nucleotide excision repair fix damaged bases. Each has to work before the DNA is replicated.Go to this step →
A MUTATIONA heritable change in the DNAA mutation is a heritable change in an organism's genetic material: a change in the chromosome that's passed to the new chromosome and the daughter cell.Go to this step →
WHERE IS IT?Location decides a lotChromosomes have genes, but also lots of DNA that doesn't code for protein. A mutation in a gene's coding region is far more likely to matter than one between genes.Go to this step →
WHAT IT DOESSilent, missense, nonsense, frameshiftIn a coding region, a change can leave the protein the same, swap one amino acid, stop it early, or scramble everything after it.Go to this step →
STEP 2 · DAMAGE AND REPAIR

What is a mutation?

A heritable change in an organism's DNA, passed on to new chromosomes and daughter cells. Watch one get made from a single mistake.

Tap the buttons, or Next step, to click through all 3
ORIGINAL DNAOur gene's first seven base pairsHere's the start of Module 2.4's gene: ATG GAA C… paired with its template. Look at the 4th pair: G·C.
1ST ROUND: AN ERRORA mismatchDuring replication, DNA polymerase puts a T opposite the G. T can't pair with G, so there's a base-pair mismatch, and the helix bulges. This is still fixable: it isn't a mutation yet.
2ND ROUND: A MUTATIONCopied into both strandsIf nobody fixes it, the next round of replication copies each strand. The strand with the T gets a new partner, A. That copy now has A·T where the original had G·C, in both strands: nothing is left to compare against. That's a mutation.In our gene, codon GAA (Glu) became AAA (Lys).
TWO CAUSES
1. Errors in cellular processes like DNA replication: spontaneous, and the most common. 2. Environmental factors (mutagens): X-rays, UV light, chemicals that damage DNA.
COMMON MIX-UP
A mismatch is not a mutation yet: there's still a correct strand to repair from. It becomes a mutation once replication copies it into both strands.
STEP 3 · DAMAGE AND REPAIR

Catching mistakes: proofreading and mismatch repair

DNA polymerase checks its own work as it goes. What it misses, a second crew finds later.

When proofreading misses one: mismatch repair

Tap the buttons, or Next step, to click through all 4
a · FIND THE MISMATCHScanning the DNASometimes DNA polymerase makes a mistake and doesn't fix it. Most cells have a backup: mismatch repair (MMR). MMR proteins scan the DNA for mismatches.
b · CUT THE NEW STRANDSome distance awayA repair enzyme breaks the backbone of the newly made strand some distance from the mismatch. The parental strand is the trusted copy.
c · REMOVE A STRETCHCorrect bases go tooAnother enzyme removes successive nucleotides, including the mismatched one, and some correct ones around it.
d · FILL IT INUsing the intact strand as a templateA DNA polymerase fills the gap by new DNA synthesis, using the intact parental strand as a template, and ligase seals the backbone. Corrected.
TWO CHECKS
Proofreading happens during replication, by DNA polymerase itself: the last base added is checked and, if wrong, removed and replaced. Mismatch repair happens after, by other enzymes that recognize mismatches DNA polymerase missed.
STEP 4 · DAMAGE AND REPAIR

How DNA gets damaged

DNA polymerase isn't the only source of trouble. Our cells have lots of repair systems, each for a specific kind of damage.

Tap the buttons, or Next step, to click through all 6
HOW CAN DNA BE DAMAGED?Five kinds of damageBesides DNA polymerase's own errors (spontaneous, the most common), mutagens damage DNA: X-rays, UV light and chemicals. Each kind of damage needs fixing before the DNA is replicated, or it can become a mutation.
SINGLE-STRAND BREAKOne backbone is cutA break in one strand's sugar-phosphate backbone.
THYMINE DIMERUV light links two TsUV light cross-links two adjacent thymines. They stop pairing with the other strand, and the helix bulges. Fixed by nucleotide excision repair.
MISSING BASEA sugar with no baseA nucleotide loses its base, leaving the sugar in the backbone.
BULKY SIDE GROUPSomething stuck to a baseA chemical attaches to a base and distorts the helix.
DOUBLE-STRAND BREAKBoth backbones cutThe chromosome is broken right through.
WHY IT'S A RACE
Damage has to be fixed before DNA replication and cell division, or the damage gets copied and passed to daughter cells as a mutation.
STEP 5 · DAMAGE AND REPAIR

Base excision repair: swap out one bad base

For a single chemically modified base: take out just that base, then rebuild one nucleotide.

Tap the buttons, or Next step, to click through all 4
a · A CHEMICALLY MODIFIED BASEUracil in DNAA base can be chemically changed. Here a U sits in the DNA where a C belongs, opposite a G. Uracil in DNA signals the repair process.
b · REMOVE JUST THE BASEDNA glycosylaseA specific enzyme for each type of modification removes just the nitrogenous base. DNA uracil glycosylase cleaves the uracil from the deoxyribose sugar.
c · REMOVE THE SUGARAP endonucleaseThe sugar-phosphate backbone is opened and the sugar is removed, leaving a one-nucleotide gap.
d · FILL AND SEALThe other strand is the templateThe other strand serves as a template, so the correct base (C, opposite G) is added. DNA ligase makes the backbone continuous to complete the repair.
BASE VS. NUCLEOTIDE EXCISION
Base excision removes just the damaged base first, then one nucleotide. Nucleotide excision breaks the backbone first and removes many nucleotides around the damage.
STEP 6 · DAMAGE AND REPAIR

UV light and nucleotide excision repair

Ultraviolet light links two neighboring thymines into a thymine dimer. A conserved repair system cuts out a whole stretch and rebuilds it.

WHY IT MATTERS
Thymine dimers lose their base pairing and make the helix bulge. In skin cells, unrepaired UV damage can cause skin cancers (carcinoma).
HOW IS THE DAMAGE FOUND?
By its shape: the enzymes detect an irregularity in the DNA structure (a distorted, bulging double helix), not a specific wrong letter.
STEP 7 · SIDE BY SIDE

Four ways to fix DNA

Same idea every time: find the problem, cut it out, rebuild from the good strand. What differs is when, what, and how much gets removed.

SystemWhenFixesRemovesWho
ProofreadingDuring replicationA wrong base just addedJust that last baseDNA polymerase itself
Mismatch repairAfter replicationMismatched base pairs DNA pol missedA stretch of the new strand, including the mismatchMMR proteins, then DNA polymerase and ligase
Base excisionBefore replicationOne chemically modified base (like U in DNA)One base, then its nucleotideA specific glycosylase, AP endonuclease, DNA polymerase, ligase
Nucleotide excisionBefore replicationBulky damage that distorts the helix (like thymine dimers)A stretch of nucleotides around the damageExcision enzymes, DNA polymerase, ligase
WHY REMOVE GOOD BASES TOO?
Mismatch repair and nucleotide excision repair can't just pluck one letter: they open the backbone and remove a stretch around the problem, correct bases included. That's fine, because the other strand is a perfect template to rebuild them.
COMMON MIX-UP
All of these use the undamaged strand as the template. If both strands are damaged at the same spot, there's nothing left to copy from.
MODULE 2.5 · PART 2

Mutations and their consequences

THE QUESTIONWhen a change slips through and gets copied, what happens to the gene, the mRNA and the protein?

Six steps: where the mutation is, point mutations and the mutation lab, insertions, deletions and frameshifts, sickle cell and cystic fibrosis, the summary with practice questions, and the character cards.

STEP 1 · WHAT A MUTATION DOES

Where the mutation is matters

A mutation in a gene that codes for protein is far more likely to hurt than one in DNA that codes for nothing.

Tap the buttons, or Next step, to click through all 6
WHERE IT IS MATTERSGenes, promoters, and the DNA betweenChromosomes contain genes, but also lots of DNA that doesn't code for proteins. The grey parts here are coding regions; the dark parts are promoters. Four mutations: which is worst?
MUT 1 · IN A CODING REGIONThe only one the ribosome readsMut 1 is the only one in a coding region, so it's the only one that can be silent, missense, nonsense or a frameshift. Whether it matters depends on what it does to the codon, and where in the protein.
MUT 2 · BETWEEN GENESThe least deleteriousNot in a promoter (so transcription is fine) and not in a coding region (so the ribosome never reads it). Likely no effect at all.
MUT 3 · IN A PROMOTERA normal protein, but maybe none of itIf transcription factors can't bind, little or no mRNA is made. The coding sequence is perfect, but there's little or no protein.
MUT 4 · IN AN INTRONCut out before translationIntrons are spliced out of the mRNA, so a change there usually doesn't reach the protein (unless it breaks the splicing itself).
WHICH STRAND IS THE TEMPLATE?Follow the arrowsGene 1 is transcribed left to right, so its template is the bottom strand (the RNA is complementary to it). Gene 2 is transcribed right to left from its promoter, so it uses the top strand.
STEP 2 · WHAT A MUTATION DOES

Point mutations: one base changes

A point mutation changes a single base pair in the DNA. If it's in a coding region, the mRNA changes, and maybe the protein. Try it on our gene.

Tap the buttons, or Next step, to click through all 4
OUR GENEBefore any mutationModule 2.4's gene: ATG GAA CGC CTC TAA. Its mRNA codes for Met, Glu, Arg, Leu, then stops. Now change one base pair at a time.
SILENT = SYNONYMOUSSame amino acidA base change that keeps the same amino acid: CUC and CUU are both Leu. The genotype changed; the phenotype didn't. Usually neutral.
MISSENSE = NON-SYNONYMOUSA different amino acidA base change that swaps one amino acid for another: Glu → Val. It changes the protein's structure; the effect can be beneficial, neutral or harmful. Even one amino acid can matter: this is the same swap as sickle cell.
NONSENSEAn early stop codonA base change that creates a stop codon: GAA → UAA. Translation stops early, and the protein is cut short (truncated): usually nonfunctional or unstable.

COMMON MIX-UP
Mutations happen in the DNA. The changed mRNA and protein are the consequences. And silent = synonymous, missense = non-synonymous: same ideas, different words.
WHICH SWAP IS WORSE?
Two missense mutations in an enzyme's active site: Val → Leu, or Val → Asp. Val → Asp is worse: Val and Leu are both nonpolar and similar in shape, while Asp is charged. A similar amino acid often still works; a very different one can wreck the active site.
STEP 3 · WHAT A MUTATION DOES

Insertions, deletions and frameshifts

What if bases are added to or deleted from the DNA? It depends on how many.

Tap the buttons, or Next step, to click through all 6
READ IN THREESLike three-letter wordsThe ribosome reads codons three bases at a time, with no gaps or spaces. What if a base is added to or deleted from the DNA?
DELETE ONEEverything after it shiftsRemove one letter and every "word" after it is read in the wrong frame. That's a frameshift.
INSERT ONESame problemAdding one letter shifts the frame too. Inserting or deleting 1 or 2 bases (not a multiple of 3) shifts the reading frame.
OUR GENE, ONE BASE ADDEDA different proteinIn a coding region, an insertion changes the way the ribosome reads all the rest of the codons. Here the stop codon is lost too.
OUR GENE, ONE BASE LOSTUsually deleteriousEvery codon after the deletion is misread: massive missense, often an early stop.
DELETE THREENo frameshiftInsert or delete a multiple of 3 and the frame is kept: amino acids are added or lost, the rest is unchanged. Cystic fibrosis is caused by exactly this (next step).

1, 3 OR 4?
1 or 4 bases: frameshift (4 isn't a multiple of 3). 3 bases: no frameshift, one amino acid added or lost. 6: two amino acids.
STEP 4 · WHAT A MUTATION DOES

Real mutations: sickle cell and cystic fibrosis

Do single amino acid changes in a protein matter? These two say yes.

Sickle-cell anemia: one base, one amino acid

Tap the buttons, or Next step, to click through all 3
A NON-SYNONYMOUS POINT MUTATIONGAG → GTGIn the gene for β-globin, a subunit of hemoglobin, one base changes: GAG → GTG. The codon becomes GUG, and glutamic acid becomes valine.
MISFOLDED HEMOGLOBINOne amino acid, a different shapeSwapping Glu for Val makes β-globin misfold. Hemoglobin crystallizes when oxygen is low, causing the cell to collapse.
SICKLE-CELL ANEMIATwo copies of the mutant genePeople who inherit two copies have sickle-cell anemia: oxygen isn't carried through the body effectively (anemia), and sickled cells block capillaries, causing pain and low oxygen levels.

Cystic fibrosis: three bases, one amino acid

Tap the buttons, or Next step, to click through all 2
A 3-NUCLEOTIDE DELETIONNo frameshiftIn the most common cystic fibrosis mutation, three nucleotides are deleted from the CFTR gene. The frame is kept, so the protein loses just one amino acid: a phenylalanine (at position 508).
A MISSING TRANSPORTERUnstable, then degradedNormal CFTR pumps chloride ions out of the cell. The mutant protein is unstable and degraded before it reaches the membrane: abnormal secretions in the lungs, liver, pancreas and other glands.
SAME SWAP AS OUR GENE
Our gene's GAA → GUA (in the mutation lab: base 5 to T) is the same kind of change as sickle cell: glutamic acid → valine. In our gene, GAA → GAG would be silent: both are Glu.
STEP 5 · SIDE BY SIDE

Point mutations, summed up

Every point mutation from this module in one table, then the slides' practice questions.

TypeWhat changesExample (coding strand TAT TGG CTA GTA CAT)Consequence
Silent = synonymousBase change that keeps the same amino acidTAT TGG → TAC TGG: Tyr Trp → Tyr TrpGenotype changes, phenotype doesn't. Usually neutral.
Missense = non-synonymousBase change that swaps one amino acid for anotherTGG → TGT: Trp → CysChanges the protein's structure: beneficial, neutral or deleterious.
NonsenseBase change that creates an early stop codonTGG → TGA: Tyr STOPProtein cut short. Usually deleterious.
FrameshiftInsertion or deletion of 1 or 2 basesTAT TCG GCT AGT ACA T: Tyr Ser Ala Ser ThrEvery codon after it misread. Usually deleterious.

Practice: a deletion in the template

Tap the buttons, or Next step, to click through all 4
PRACTICEA deletion in the templateThe template strand at the start of a coding region is 5′–TACTGGGATAGCCTTCCAT–3′. In a mutant, the T marked * is deleted. What will this most likely cause?
1 · WRITE THE mRNAComplementary, antiparallelPair every base and reverse the direction: 5′–AUG GAA GGC UAU CCC AGU A–3′. It starts with AUG, and it's Met, Glu, Gly, Tyr, Pro, Ser.
2 · FIND THE SHIFTOne base lostThe deleted template T removes an A from the mRNA's second codon. One base lost (not a multiple of 3), so every codon after it is read in the wrong frame.
3 · THE ANSWERb. codons after the mutation are misreadA deletion causing a frameshift in the coding region. Bonus: RNA polymerase reads the template 3′ → 5′, so transcription goes right to left as written.
A gene's first RNA is 12,000 nucleotides; its mature mRNA is 3,000; its protein is 600 amino acids. Which is FALSE? (C) "The gene is now only 3,000 base pairs long because the introns were removed from the DNA."

C is false. Splicing removes introns from the RNA; the DNA never changes. And 600 amino acids need 1,800 nucleotides, so about 1,200 nucleotides of the mRNA aren't translated (UTRs).

A tRNA has the anticodon 5′–CGU–3′. Which amino acid does it carry?

Thr. The codon is complementary and antiparallel: 5′–ACG–3′. Codon tables are always read 5′ → 3′: ACG = threonine.

Most mRNAs in a mutant cell line are longer than normal, but the proteins are the same size. One mutation. Where is it most likely?

In the RNA polymerase gene, so the polymerase no longer responds to termination signals: transcripts run on past the end, but the stop codons are untouched, so the proteins are normal. (A stop codon mutation would only affect one gene.)

STEP 6 · CARDS

The repair crew, and what mutations hit

Seven characters: four repair enzymes, the damage they fix, and two proteins famous for their mutations.

MUTATION · 1 / 71

Mismatch repair proteins

THE SPELL-CHECKER
Scanning newly copied DNA
POWERFind base pairs that don't match after replication, and get the wrong base cut out (with a stretch around it) and rebuilt from the parental strand.
IF IT'S MISSINGDNA polymerase's uncaught errors get copied in the next round: more mutations.
MUTATION · 2 / 72

DNA glycosylase

THE BASE PLUCKER
Base excision repair · one kind for each kind of damaged base
POWERRemoves just the base of a chemically modified nucleotide (like uracil in DNA), leaving the sugar.
IF IT'S MISSINGThe damaged base stays and can be misread at the next replication.
MUTATION · 3 / 73

AP endonuclease

THE GAP OPENER
Base excision repair
POWERCuts the backbone where a base is missing and removes the sugar, so DNA polymerase can put in the right nucleotide.
IF IT'S MISSINGBaseless sugars stay in the backbone: no clean gap to repair.
MUTATION · 4 / 74

Excision enzymes

THE BULGE FINDER
Nucleotide excision repair
POWERDetect an irregular, bulging double helix, cut the damaged strand on both sides, and remove a whole stretch of nucleotides.
IF IT'S MISSINGThymine dimers aren't removed: UV damage builds up (in skin cells, a cause of skin cancer).
MUTATION · 5 / 75

Thymine dimer

THE UV GLITCH
Made by UV light, on one strand
WHAT IT ISTwo adjacent thymines linked together by UV light. They lose their pairing with the other strand, and the helix bulges.
FIXED BYNucleotide excision repair: cut out and rebuilt from the other strand.
MUTATION · 6 / 76

Hemoglobin

THE OXYGEN CARRIER
In red blood cells
POWERCarries oxygen through the body. Made of subunits, including β-globin.
IF IT'S MUTATEDOne base in β-globin (GAG → GTG) swaps Glu for Val: it misfolds and crystallizes at low oxygen. Two copies: sickle-cell anemia.
MUTATION · 7 / 77

CFTR

THE CHLORIDE PUMP
In the cell membrane
POWERA transporter that pumps chloride ions out of the cell.
IF IT'S MUTATEDLosing three nucleotides (one Phe) makes it unstable: it's degraded before reaching the membrane. That's cystic fibrosis.
